podcast.title: 3 AM Inspiration for "Shop Around"
podcast.body: After two unsuccessful versions, Barry Gordy had a sudden realization at 3 AM that The Miracles' "Shop Around" needed a new, faster arrangement. His immediate action to call Smokey Robinson and get the group into the studio led to the song becoming a number two pop hit and a million-seller. "then at 3 o'clock in the morning Barry Gordy had suddenly realised that the record needed a new, faster arrangement."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Evolution of Motown's Slogan
podcast.body: Barry Gordy initially coined the Motown slogan "create, make, and sell" to reflect his goal of producing great records that sold widely. However, recognizing the financial challenges of unpaid distributors, he revised it to "create, sell, and collect," emphasizing the crucial importance of securing payment. "He changed that slogan to create, sell, and collect."

podcast.title: Production of The Fidelitones
podcast.body: In the late 1950s, before Motown's major success, Barry Gordy produced several unreleased tracks for The Fidelitones on the Aladdin label, featuring future Motown talents Brian Holland and Freddie Gorman. "The Fidelitones had recorded some tracks for Aladdin, produced by Gordy in the late 50s, but they'd never been released."

podcast.title: Renaming The Marvelettes
podcast.body: Barry Gordy is credited with giving The Marvelettes their definitive name. After hearing the group, then known as The Cassin Yet, he supposedly remarked, "those girls are marvels," leading to their new identity. "The name they were eventually given supposedly came after Barry Gordy heard them sing it and said, those girls are marvels."

podcast.title: Signing The Primettes (The Supremes)
podcast.body: Motown staff widely believed that Barry Gordy signed The Primettes (later The Supremes) more due to his attraction to member Diane Ross than for the group's talent, despite their initial lack of success. "Motown had already signed one girl group, a group called The Primates, who had been renamed and who had so far released two singles. But the Supremes, as they were renamed, wouldn't become successful for several years, and were generally regarded as a joke among the Motown staff, who thought, not entirely without reason, that they had been signed more because Barry Gordy was attracted to Diane Ross, one of the members of the group, than because of any talent they had."
